                  Academia Litterarum Regia Borussica (Royal Prussian

     Print Basis: Berlin: apud Georgium Reimerum (Reimer), MDCCCXCIV
                  (1894). This is the Numidia supplement fascicle of
                  CIL VIII, not the 1881 main volume itself -- Donatism
                  world-build Source_Acquisition_Manifest.md §1
                  request G7 named "vol. VIII... with supplements" as
                  the acceptable range, and Numidia is this world's
                  own Donatist heartland province.
          Rights: Public Domain
        Language: lat
    Rights basis: 1894 publication date places this volume long out of
                  US copyright. The scan's own front matter states
                  explicitly: "In compliance with current copyright
                  law, the University of Minnesota Bindery produced
                  this facsimile on permanent-durable paper to replace
                  the irreparably deteriorated original volume owned
                  by the University Library. 1991" -- a 1991
                  preservation facsimile of the 1894 original, not a
                  new copyrighted edition.
Source Collection: Internet Archive / Google Books scan. Supplied
                  2026-09-01 as a DOCX file attachment, converted
                  mechanically via a zip/XML text extraction (paragraph
                  boundaries preserved from </w:p> splits) - no content
                  passed through model-generated output. This paste's
                  own leading archive.org chrome was minimal ("Full
                  text of ..." / "See other formats" - 2 lines,
                  stripped at vendoring); everything after that is
                  unedited raw OCR output.
      Confirmed find: this world's own Source_Registry.md row 27 (the
                  "Deo laudes" acclamation) had stood at Confidence C,
                  a recognized field category with no specific
                  catalogued inscription, since this Registry's first
                  draft. This volume's own editorial apparatus directly
                  resolves that gap. The primary witness is inscription
                  no. 17732, found on two pillars near Bagai itself
                  (now preserved at Khenchela) and reading "DEO LAVDES"
                  twice; the editors' own note there reads, in full,
                  "Uti [Deo] gratias... catholicorum, ita [Deo] laudes
                  signum ac tessera fuit Donatistarum, quorum sedes
                  primariae erant Bagai et Thamugadi" -- "just as 'Deo
                  gratias' [was the sign] of Catholics, so 'Deo laudes'
                  was the sign and token of the Donatists, whose
                  primary seats were Bagai and Thamugadi." A second
                  inscription, no. 20482 ("DEO LAVDES SVPER AQVAS..."),
                  carries an editorial note that is a direct
                  cross-reference back to 17732's own identification --
                  "Deo laudes (de hoc signo Donatistarum cf. supra ad
                  n. 17732)" -- not a second, independent attestation;
                  20482 is itself found at Beni Fouda, in this same
                  volume's own Mauretania Sitifensis supplement
                  section, not the Numidian material proper (an
                  earlier version of this note misdescribed it as
                  "found near Constantine," corrected 2026-09-02 on
                  direct re-reading of the surrounding heading, which
                  reads "MAVRETANIA SITIFENSIS SVPPL."). Two further
                  inscriptions in this same volume also carry the
                  acclamation: no. 17368 ("DEO LAVDES") and no. 18669
                  ("DEO LAVDES DICAMVS"). Correction, 2026-09-02: an
                  earlier version of this note stated inscription
                  17732 "was not found in this specific volume" --
                  that was a search error; 17732 is present in this
                  volume's own Bagai section (in the Bagai/Khenchela
                  region entries) and is in fact the strongest of the
                  four attestations, not a missing cross-reference.
     OCR quality: Raw, uncorrected OCR of a dense 19th-century
                  epigraphic reference work using heavy Latin
                  apparatus abbreviation and a critical typeface this
                  OCR handles poorly -- expect substantial letter
                  substitution and garbling throughout, worse than the
                  narrative-prose texts elsewhere in this corpus. Any
                  specific inscription number or reading pulled from
                  this file needs visual cross-check against its own
                  surrounding context, and ideally against a standard
                  CIL concordance, before being relied on for a
                  verbatim claim.
